pitchHistory.title: The Minecraft Movie Wasn't Supposed to Work — So Why Did It Break the Internet?
pitchHistory.summary: The Minecraft movie adaptation arrived with all the energy of a corporate PowerPoint and somehow became the most culturally alive thing to happen to cinema in years — not despite its absurdity, but because of it. This post unpacks why the film's chaotic audience response (the screaming, the throwing, the unhinged theatrical rituals) is less about the movie itself and more about a generation that grew up inside a game and finally got to perform that identity in public. It's a story about nostalgia as a social technology, and why the internet didn't just watch the Minecraft movie — it became part of it.

pitchHistory.title: RIP Memes (2009–2025): Why the Internet Is Trying to Reboot Itself Back to 2016
pitchHistory.summary: The 'Great Meme Reset' — a viral movement demanding internet culture revert to pre-brainrot, pre-AI 2016 memes — sounds like a joke, but it's actually a genuine symptom of something worth taking seriously: the industrialisation of humour. When memes have a 48-hour shelf life, when AI slops out ten thousand 'Italian Brainrot' creatures before breakfast, and when every brand is in your comments doing the bit, what does it mean that people are nostalgically reaching for Trollface like it's a lost golden age? This post unpacks what the Meme Reset reveals about authenticity, algorithmic anxiety, and why the internet keeps trying to escape itself.

pitchHistory.title: The Vampires Were Always the Music Industry: How 'Sinners' Became the Horror Film That Ate Hollywood
pitchHistory.summary: Ryan Coogler's 1930s Mississippi vampire epic just won 4 Oscars, broke records with 16 nominations, and grossed nearly $400 million — but the real story is what's hiding inside the genre clothes: a full-throated argument about who gets to own Black music, told through blues guitar and bloodsuckers. This post unpacks why 'Sinners' isn't just a great horror film but a cultural thesis statement arriving at exactly the right moment, and what it means that Hollywood's most self-congratulatory night finally had to reckon with it.

pitchHistory.title: YouTube Ate Hollywood and Nobody Noticed: The Sidemen, MrBeast, and the Creator-to-Netflix Pipeline That's Rewriting the Rules of Fame
pitchHistory.summary: The Sidemen's 'Inside' just dropped on Netflix, MrBeast has been colonising streaming for years, and the old line between 'influencer' and 'prestige content' has quietly dissolved — so what does it mean when the people who built their empires by being parasocially accessible to millions are now playing by Hollywood's rules? This post digs into the creator economy's hostile takeover of traditional entertainment, why Netflix keeps writing cheques to YouTubers, and what it reveals about how attention, loyalty, and stardom have been fundamentally rewired in the algorithmic age.

pitchHistory.title: Valerie Cherish Saw It Coming: How 'The Comeback' Became the Most Accidentally Prophetic Show on Television
pitchHistory.summary: HBO's 'The Comeback' returned after 11+ years with Lisa Kudrow's Valerie Cherish starring in Hollywood's first AI-written sitcom — a premise so perfectly timed it landed the same week the WGA signed a new contract specifically to limit AI in writers' rooms. This post argues that 'The Comeback' has now done it three times: debuted in 2005 mocking reality TV before reality TV ate everything, returned in 2014 to skewer streaming prestige culture right as it peaked, and come back in 2026 as a brutal comedy about AI displacement — except this time, the satire isn't ahead of the curve, it *is* the curve. It's the rare show that doesn't just reflect the culture; it keeps arriving at exactly the right moment to tell us what we're too uncomfortable to say straight.

pitchHistory.title: Euphoria Grew Up. That's the Problem.
pitchHistory.summary: Euphoria Season 3 premiered today after a four-year hiatus, and critics are already asking the question nobody wanted to say out loud: was the show ever actually profound, or was it just glamorous chaos wearing a philosophy degree? The real answer is more interesting — Euphoria's cultural stranglehold was never really about drugs or drama or glitter eyeliner. It was about the specific, intoxicating terror of being a teenager, and the show only worked because it weaponised youth itself as an aesthetic. Now the characters are adults and suddenly everyone's noticing the emperor has no clothes — which says something pretty unsettling about why we were watching in the first place.

pitchHistory.title: The Algorithm Made Me Like This Band: The Geese 'Psyop' and the Death of Organic Music Discovery
pitchHistory.summary: This week, a viral WIRED exposé revealed that Brooklyn rock band Geese — hailed as America's most thrilling young band and fresh off a Coachella slot — hired a boutique firm to manufacture their social media buzz through fake fan accounts and engineered TikTok campaigns. It's the perfect hook into a much bigger story: in 2026, 'organic discovery' is almost entirely a myth, and every algorithm is a pay-to-play shelf where the artists with marketing budgets get the eye-level placement. The post asks the uncomfortable question nobody in music Twitter wants to answer — if the vibe is manufactured but the songs still slap, does it even matter?

pitchHistory.title: The Crowd Goes Wild While the Critics Wince: What the 'Michael' Biopic Tells Us About How We Actually Consume Art
pitchHistory.summary: The Michael Jackson biopic just opened to $217 million worldwide despite near-universal critical contempt — and that gap isn't just a story about bad taste, it's a story about how we've split into two entirely separate audiences living in different moral universes. This post digs into why sanitised hagiobiopics keep printing money, what it reveals about the psychology of fan loyalty vs. critical accountability, and whether the 'Bohemian Rhapsody effect' has permanently broken the link between quality and blockbuster success.

pitchHistory.title: When the Machine Touches the Sacred: Soderbergh, Lennon, and the AI Controversy Cannes Can't Escape
pitchHistory.summary: Steven Soderbergh just admitted that 10% of his John Lennon documentary — premiering at Cannes next week — was generated by AI, and the internet has had precisely the reaction you'd expect. This is the perfect case study for the real question haunting every creative industry right now: not whether AI can make art, but whether it's allowed to touch the icons we've decided are untouchable — and what it reveals about our deeply inconsistent feelings about authenticity, authorship, and who gets to own a dead genius.

pitchHistory.title: Netflix Just Made Animal Farm. Orwell Is Spinning in His Grave — and He Might Be Wrong To.
pitchHistory.summary: Netflix's new animated Animal Farm has landed in 2026 and the discourse is already a mess: purists furious about the changes, others arguing that adapting Orwell for an algorithm-fed global audience is exactly the kind of ideological test the book was written about. This post digs into what it means when the streaming-industrial complex — a system Orwell would have had opinions about — becomes the custodian of anti-totalitarian art, and whether the irony is damning or actually kind of perfect.

pitchHistory.title: The Festival That Banned AI While Being Sponsored By It: What Cannes 2026 Actually Proved
pitchHistory.summary: The 79th Cannes Film Festival officially banned generative AI from competition, had Guillermo del Toro denouncing it from the Croisette, and protesters waving 'Fuck AI' placards — while Meta and Kling AI were major sponsors and a parallel AI Film Festival ran *inside* the Palais. Then Demi Moore told Hollywood to stop 'fighting' AI and the internet lost its mind. This post unpacks the spectacular institutional hypocrisy at the heart of cinema's most glamorous week, and asks the genuinely interesting question underneath the noise: can any cultural institution credibly draw a line around tools when the money flowing through it has already crossed it?

pitchHistory.title: The Government Used Olivia Rodrigo's Most Pointed Song as Propaganda — and Somehow Made It More Powerful
pitchHistory.summary: This week, Rodrigo went on record calling it 'deeply disturbing': the DHS used 'All-American Bitch' — a song about the suffocating performance of female perfection — in a deportation propaganda video, without her permission. It's a perfect, almost satirical collision of pop stardom, state power, and the question of who gets to own a song's meaning once it's out in the world. With her new album dropping June 12 and Sabrina Carpenter's music getting the same treatment, this isn't a one-off — it's a pattern worth taking seriously, and it raises something genuinely weird about why governments keep reaching for Gen Z anthems to do their dirty work.
